transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Alright, thanks everyone for making time, I know critique sessions can run long so I want to be disciplined about pacing today. Goal is to land on a direction for the grid system before we hand this to engineering.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sounds good, I've got about forty five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Same, and thanks for having me, I've got some direct customer language to bring in when it's useful.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: And I'm here mostly to poke at feasibility, so feel free to get excited about ideas, I'll just flag when something's a bigger lift than it looks.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Perfect, that's exactly the role I want you playing. Okay, quick recap for context, the research from our last round of interviews was clear, people want customizable widget layouts, drag and drop, basically a bento box style dashboard instead of our current fixed grid.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yeah, Northstar specifically asked about this in their last QBR, their ops team wants bigger charts for the metrics they care about and smaller tiles for stuff they just glance at.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Exactly the use case we're designing for. I've got three directions mocked up, let me share my screen and walk through them.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Go for it.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Option one is a strict twelve column grid, widgets snap to column boundaries, resize in increments, pretty structured. Option two is a freeform canvas, widgets can go anywhere, any size, much more flexible but way less guided. Option three is a hybrid, twelve column grid but with more granular row heights so things feel less blocky.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: My gut reaction, freeform canvas is going to be a nightmare to build well, collision detection, overlap resolution, that's a lot of edge cases for something that might not even look better.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: That's actually where I landed too after building all three, freeform looked exciting in Figma but every time I tried to imagine real usage, I kept picturing overlapping widgets and a messy end state.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: From a customer support angle I'd also worry about that, a mess is a mess whether we built it well or not, if customers can make their dashboard look chaotic, some of them will.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Agreed, I think we rule out freeform. Between the strict grid and the hybrid, what's actually different day to day for a user?

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: The hybrid gives finer control over widget height specifically, so a chart with a legend can be slightly taller than one without, without eating a whole extra row. The strict grid version, every widget in a row is the same height, which felt a bit rigid in testing.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: How much more complex is the hybrid to build compared to the strict version?

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know exactly, that's actually the question I wanted your read on.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Let me think out loud. The strict twelve column, fixed row height version, that's a pretty well trodden pattern, there are solid open source grid libraries we could build on. The hybrid with variable row heights per widget, that's more custom logic, especially for how widgets reflow when one changes height.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Is it double the work, triple, or more like twenty percent more?

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Rough guess, maybe forty to fifty percent more engineering time for the hybrid, mostly in the reflow logic and making resize handles feel good when heights aren't uniform.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: That's useful to know. Is there a middle ground, strict grid for the MVP, and we look at variable row heights as a fast follow once the core interaction is proven out?

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Yeah, I actually like that a lot better than trying to nail both at once. Ship the well-trodden pattern first, learn from real usage, then invest in the more custom reflow behavior if it turns out people actually want it.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'm on board with that sequencing, gets us something real faster and de-risks the harder engineering problem.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: That works from a customer angle too honestly, even the strict grid version is already a big upgrade from what we have today, which is basically zero customization.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Great, let's lock that, strict twelve column grid for v1, variable row heights as a fast follow candidate. Let's talk resize behavior next, this is where a lot of the ambiguity lives.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Yeah, this actually came up in an interview I was on recently, the candidate specifically flagged resize edge cases as something that needs explicit spec before building, so glad we're doing this now.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Ha, good, that means it's a real gap and not just me overthinking it. Okay, first question, minimum widget size. What's the smallest a widget can be resized to?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd think about it from readability, a single stat tile probably needs less space than a full chart with axis labels.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Agreed, I'm proposing two size tiers as a floor, a one by one unit minimum for stat tiles, and a two by two minimum for anything with a chart, so labels and legends don't get crushed.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: That's implementable, as long as the grid system enforces that per widget type rather than a single global minimum, which is a bit more setup but not hard.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Good, let's spec it per widget type then. Next, what happens when you resize a widget and it would overlap a neighbor, does it push the neighbor down, or just block the resize?

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Push is more forgiving for users but harder to build predictably, especially cascading pushes where pushing one widget pushes another below it. Block is way simpler technically but can feel frustrating if you're trying to make something bigger and it just won't budge.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: From what customers described, I think they'd expect push behavior, that's basically how most drag and drop tools they've used elsewhere work, like Trello boards or even Notion.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I agree push feels like the expected behavior, but Sofia, if that's a meaningfully bigger lift, I don't want to force it if it delays the whole feature.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: It's more work but not wildly more, most grid libraries have push-based reflow built in as a feature, we'd mostly be configuring behavior rather than building it from scratch. I'm comfortable committing to push behavior for v1.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Great, that settles it, push behavior on resize and drag, using whatever the underlying library gives us for reflow logic. Let's talk about drag interactions specifically, is it drag the whole widget by clicking anywhere on it, or a dedicated drag handle?

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I'd lean dedicated handle honestly, if you drag from anywhere, it's easy to accidentally trigger a drag when someone's just trying to click into a chart to filter it or hover for a tooltip.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Agreed from an implementation angle too, a dedicated handle avoids a bunch of gesture conflict edge cases with clicks and hovers inside the widget.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Okay, dedicated drag handle in the widget header then, I'll design that as a small grip icon that appears on hover so it's not visual clutter all the time.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works, keeps things clean until someone's actually trying to rearrange.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Let's talk about saving and layout persistence. Is layout saved automatically as you move things, or is there an explicit save action?

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Auto save is friendlier, but we should debounce it so we're not firing a save request on every pixel of drag movement, more like save a second or two after the user stops interacting.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Good, auto save with debounce, no explicit save button. What about multiple layouts, can a user have more than one saved arrangement, or just one active layout?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd keep it simple for v1, one layout per user, we can revisit multiple named layouts later if people ask for it, I don't want to add complexity nobody's requested yet.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Agreed, nobody's actually asked me for multiple layouts specifically, they just want to arrange the one dashboard they look at daily.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Good, one layout per user for now. Let's talk about default state, what does a brand new user see before they've customized anything?

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think we should ship with a sensible default layout, not an empty grid, something that shows the widgets most customers actually use based on usage data, so it's useful on day one.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: That's important, a blank canvas on day one would probably confuse a lot of less technical users, especially at accounts like Globex where not everyone's comfortable building dashboards from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Agreed, I'll design a default arrangement using our top five most-viewed widget types as a starting template, and users can rearrange or remove from there.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: That's straightforward to implement, we already have usage analytics on which widgets get viewed most, so the default template can be data driven rather than a guess.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Perfect. Okay, I think we've resolved the big open questions. Let me recap what we've decided, strict twelve column grid for v1, push-based resize and drag behavior, per-widget-type minimum sizes, dedicated drag handle in the widget header, auto save with debounce, one layout per user, and a data driven default layout for new users.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: That's a really solid, well-scoped v1, nothing on that list feels like scope creep.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Agreed, and honestly having all these decisions explicit means engineering won't be guessing or blocked waiting on design mid-sprint.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: This is going to be a great story for our next round of customer conversations, especially Northstar.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Great, let's talk next steps. I'll turn these decisions into a proper spec document with annotated mocks for each interaction we discussed.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Once that's ready I can size the engineering work more precisely and we can slot it into an upcoming sprint, probably worth flagging to Derek given how it might compete with the alerting work for engineering time.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Good call, I'll loop Derek in once the spec's done so he can plan capacity.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: And I'd love to preview the spec with a couple of design partner customers before engineering starts building, just to sanity check before we invest real engineering time.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I can set that up, Northstar would probably be thrilled to be a design partner on this given how much they've been asking for it.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Perfect, let's do that. I'll have the spec doc ready by end of week, Aisha can you line up the Northstar preview for early next week once it's ready?

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yep, I'll reach out to them today so we have a slot booked.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Great, and Sofia, once you've seen the finished spec, can you get me a rough sizing estimate so we know what we're asking Derek to fit into the roadmap?

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Yeah, I'll turn that around within a couple days of getting the spec.

transcript.speaker: Tom Bennett
transcript.text: Perfect, I think that's everything. This was a really productive session, thank you all for the sharp feedback, especially the push-versus-block resize discussion, that could easily have been a mid-sprint fire drill if we hadn't nailed it down now.

transcript.speaker: Maya Chen
transcript.text: Agreed, great use of the time, thanks Tom.

transcript.speaker: Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Thanks everyone, excited to bring this to Northstar.

transcript.speaker: Sofia Marin
transcript.text: Thanks all, talk soon.

summary.overview: Tom led a design critique session with Maya, Aisha, and Sofia to finalize the direction for Beacon's drag-and-drop dashboard grid redesign. The group ruled out a freeform canvas layout as too complex and risky, instead choosing a strict 12-column grid for v1 with variable row heights considered as a fast follow. Key interaction decisions were locked in: push-based collision behavior on resize and drag, per-widget-type minimum sizes, a dedicated drag handle, auto-save with debounce, one layout per user, and a data-driven default layout for new users. The session closed with clear next steps: a full spec document, an engineering sizing pass from Sofia, and a preview session with Northstar as a design partner.
bullet_points: ❌ Freeform canvas layout ruled out; too complex, risk of messy end states
📐 Strict 12-column grid chosen for v1, variable row heights deferred as a fast follow (~40-50% more engineering effort)
🧩 Minimum widget sizes set per type: 1x1 for stat tiles, 2x2 for chart widgets
↔️ Push-based collision behavior confirmed for resize and drag (not block)
🖱️ Dedicated drag handle in widget header, appears on hover
💾 Auto-save with debounce, one layout per user for v1
🆕 New users get a data-driven default layout based on top 5 most-viewed widgets
🤝 Northstar to preview the spec as a design partner before engineering build starts
